# Applications: Wearable Technology: Athlete Analytics (SSAC15 panel)

## Where this applies

- Inference: The panel's point that coaches need one simplified number, with a light or hard mechanical day described in plain words [16:23], suggests a coach-facing daily tier for football (for example light, moderate, hard) built from GPS player load against each athlete's own recent history. Show it to the strength coach before it reaches position coaches.
- Inference: The panel's argument that individual limits can replace fixed rules like a flat pitch count [17:23] maps to athletes with a hamstring history. A per-athlete ceiling on high-speed running or accelerations, reviewed with Athletic Medicine, could be compared with the team default over a season.
- Inference: The days-lost metric [57:35] gives a simple outcome to judge monitoring against. Counting days lost by position group and cause (with Athletic Medicine's records) is a cheap way to ask whether the GPS and VALD work is changing availability.
- Inference: The ACL-return example, where reduced cutting to one side signaled he was not ready [59:07], suggests checking left-right asymmetry in change-of-direction counts for athletes returning from knee injury, alongside VALD force plate asymmetry, as one more readiness signal for Athletic Medicine.
- Inference: The disagreement among panelists on what to tell athletes [50:02], [51:32] means Baylor should have an explicit rule for which numbers athletes see and when, rather than leaving it to each coach.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: Catapult is the GPS stack, Kitman Labs the central data store, VALD the force plate suite (Playbook p.7). The panel names Catapult as a vendor and describes the same core idea (load, speed, distance); it agrees but adds nothing specific.
- Eric's baseline: Eric's writing describes dropping daily subjective wellness surveys because athletes learned to game them, and keeping objective daily force plate (mRSI) data. The panel is mixed: several speakers lean on objective numbers, but one says coaches' eyes are accurate and data mainly confirms them [18:55]. The course material also argues for a good coach's eye. The panel extends the tension between coach's eye and objective data that the baseline lists (Tension 3); it does not resolve it.
- Eric's baseline: Injury risk is reduced, not eliminated. The panel's most concrete claim, a hamstring-history player who stayed healthy once capped [07:10], is a single case and does not support a stronger claim than that.
- Eric's baseline: The course material criticizes load monitoring for producing a fear-driven culture of under-training. The panel's first example is a workload cap, but one speaker also says the technology is not just for backing athletes off [15:21]. Partly conflicts, partly agrees.
- Eric's baseline: Data collection should stop when the insight no longer justifies the cost; a valid test needs staff ownership and consistent collection. The panel's point that hardware is cheap but the service around it is costly [49:01] agrees.

## What would have to be true

- Several seasons of consistent GPS wear and clean tagging, so each athlete has a stable baseline.
- Athletic Medicine injury records with a shared definition of days lost and cause.
- Enough athletes per position group to compare capped and uncapped cases; one athlete is an anecdote.
- Coach buy-in on what the tier means, agreed before the season.

## Do not apply when

- Treating any vendor's claims as evidence. Three of the five panelists sell or are tied to wearables companies, and their examples are anecdotes.
- Reading the Australian live-substitution example [34:16] as permission for in-game use at Baylor. The panel says college use was only being viewed live, not acted on [35:17]; check conference rules.
- Applying pro contract or salary-cap reasoning [28:41], [29:12] to college athletes.
- Using the pick-and-roll and knee injury idea [54:34] for anything. The speaker called it not a fact.
- Relying on the Antonio Bryant story [59:37] for medical or contract reasoning; it is a hedged anecdote.

## First step

For one football position group, take last season's session loads and label each day light, moderate or hard retrospectively against that athlete's rolling average. Compare the labels with days Athletic Medicine recorded lost. Change nothing about practice.

# Applications: How in Game Use of Wearables Increases the Predictive Injury Analytics (SSAC16)

This talk was given by Baylor staff in 2016, so it shows how the program described its own practice at that time. Whether the practices below are still current is something only Eric can say.

## Where this applies

- Inference: The position-specific metric choices [12:38], [13:38] (player load per yard for linemen, accelerations and decelerations and low-velocity IMA for linemen, high-velocity distance for skill players) can be checked against the current Baylor football data dictionary, which the baseline says has no position-specific thresholds. Build the position tables from Catapult data already held.
- Inference: The weekly load shape (Tuesday and Wednesday at 60 to 70 percent of game load, Thursday at 50 to 55 percent [17:16], [17:48]) is a ready-made check. Compute the current-season shape per position group and see whether it still matches, and whether outliers line up with Athletic Medicine events.
- Inference: The preparedness idea (compare today to the last three or four weeks, not to last year's camp [10:38]) gives a rolling-baseline rule for flagging spikes in high-velocity distance and changes of direction for each athlete.
- Inference: The body-weight and speed link [11:08], [12:08] suggests a per-athlete table of body mass against top speed (GPS or VALD) so Performance Nutrition gets a target weight range with evidence for each skill-position athlete.
- Inference: The mood and RPE mismatch [09:07] could be used only as a conversation prompt for return-to-play athletes, where the baseline keeps subjective monitoring.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: Preparedness (long-built capability) is distinguished from readiness (day-to-day fluctuation) in the course material (speaker unconfirmed). The talk agrees, and extends it with a practical rule: preparedness from recent weeks of exposure [10:38].
- Eric's baseline: Speed needs re-exposure about every 5 days, strength and aerobic about every 30 days (course material, speaker unconfirmed). The talk says speed every 7 to 10 days and strength about weekly [06:04]. Conflicts on the numbers, although the two may measure different things (residual effect versus training cadence); the talk does not say.
- Eric's baseline: Eric's writing describes dropping daily subjective wellness surveys after about a year because athletes learned to game them, and moving to objective force plate mRSI, while keeping surveys for return to play and chronic conditions. The talk's reliance on self-report mood, soreness and sleep questionnaires [21:54] conflicts with that later position for general roster use, though the talk predates it and uses the questionnaires to start conversations.
- Eric's baseline: The aerobic system's main value for speed-power athletes is recovery between efforts (class transcript, speaker unconfirmed). The talk's description of the aerobic system as a recycling system [23:25] agrees.
- Eric's baseline: Core GPS metrics at Baylor include player load, IMA, heart-rate bands and velocity bands (Playbook). The talk agrees on the metric list and adds position-specific uses. Performance Nutrition owns body composition; the talk's suggestion to hand nutrition a target weight [11:38] fits that split.

## What would have to be true

- Several seasons of consistent Catapult data per position group, with the same device placement and filters.
- Enough athletes per position and per week to compare against the 100 percent game-load reference; a single game load can be unusual.
- A clear way to match load spikes to Athletic Medicine events with consistent injury definitions.
- Body mass and top speed recorded close together in time for each athlete.

## Do not apply when

- Treating the talk's observations (mood changes perceived effort, nutrition leads to a sleep and weight spiral) as findings. No data, n or statistics were shown; they were described as seen over three years [12:08].
- Reading the weekly load percentages as targets for another team, schedule or offense; they come from one program in one season's schedule.
- Taking the 25 percent spike tolerance [11:08] as a rule; the captions are ambiguous (25 or 50 percent) and no evidence was given.
- Treating the line-of-scrimmage claim that tackles turn outside 70 percent of the time [14:10] as grounds to train the opposite direction; the speakers themselves said there are two schools of thought.
- Expecting this talk to show in-game wearable use or a predictive model. It shows neither.

## First step

Pull last season's Tuesday through Thursday player load as a percent of game load for wide receivers. Compare it with the 60 to 70 and 50 to 55 percent figures from the talk. Note the gap for yourself; no action required.

---
type: video-summary
video_id: PX_N6MpkHTg
title: "SSAC15: Amateurs or Industry: NCAA Reform"
event: SSAC15 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Warren Zola (moderator), Oliver Luck, Mike mccan (caption spelling), Jim Phillips, Rod Thorne (caption spelling), Amal mapani (caption spelling; student host)]
topics: [policy, american-football, basketball]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

A 2015 panel of NCAA, university, law and NBA voices debates how college sports should change as money, lawsuits and the Power 5 split reshape the amateur model. Panelists discuss whether athletes are employees under labor law, an antitrust challenge to scholarship caps, Title IX limits on paying revenue-sport athletes, the NBA age rule, and the role of agents. Most speakers favor gradual recalibration over abolition, with more weight on academics and athlete health and welfare. No analytics or data models are shown. The value for a performance staff is the policy context that shapes eligibility, time demands and what athlete data collection could mean legally.

## Key claims

- Jim Phillips (Northwestern) says campus athletics exists to teach skills such as teamwork that a classroom does not, and that academics must be the base of any reform. [03:37]
- Oliver Luck says he joined the NCAA because he thinks the college model is unique in the world and worth saving while reforming what is broken. [06:11]
- Rod Thorne (NBA, caption spelling) says the league's concern is player health, including very dense schedules, and that the injury level is no higher than in recent years. [08:15]
- Mike mccan (caption spelling) explains that if football players are declared employees, a separate vote is still needed to unionize, and a ruling could let athletes at other private schools rely on it. [10:17] [10:47]
- Mike notes the employee question is tricky because only some athletes (football) might unionize, leaving others unclear. [11:17]
- Jim lists recent reforms: unlimited meals, full cost of attendance, four-year grants. [13:19]
- Jim asks whether seasons are too long and time demands too high, and mentions a "year of readiness" idea that needs study. [13:51] [14:21]
- A panelist, citing a former NCAA president, says amateurism is a social construct that changes by era. [16:23]
- A panelist says cost of attendance is a federal calculation done by each school's financial aid office and that athletes have been under-resourced for decades. [18:26] [19:29]
- Rod says the NBA one-year rule is a disaster for colleges but better for the NBA than drafting from high school; the league would prefer two years but needs the Players Association. [22:31] [23:03] [23:35]
- Mike says those hurt by eligibility rules have no seat at the bargaining table, and a legal challenge to the age rule would likely also name the union. [24:05] [25:07]
- Oliver says rules on agents may be liberalized so athletes get better information, with a warning that some advice would be self-serving. [27:38] [28:39]
- Jim says realignment was partly driven by finances, and that nearly all programs lose money without institutional subsidy. [30:42] [31:11]
- Mike expects Title IX litigation if men's basketball and football players are paid. [33:14]
- Mike says the Jenkins antitrust case could be a game changer, but stars would gain while many athletes might not exceed the value of a scholarship. [35:48] [36:19]
- Schools are budgeting for a trust fund per year under a judge's order (caption: "oanon" case, judge "wilin"). [34:16] [34:46]
- Predictions: Oliver sees a healthy enterprise with more liberalization and academic emphasis [38:24]; Mike sees a trust-fund compromise and a capped, group-negotiated name and likeness model [39:24] [40:28]; Jim hopes pro-bound athletes get non-college options such as training academies [42:32]; Rod says the NBA's minor league could play a larger role [44:35].
- Jim says schools made decisions that were not in athletes' interest, and that graduation rates and academic standards either matter or they do not. [53:51] [54:53]
- A panelist says a single national academic cutoff is hard because campuses differ in mission. [55:24]
- Mike says coaches, not presidents or athletic directors, often hold the decision power, unlike in pro leagues. [56:55] [57:27]

## Numbers and definitions

- About 2.7 to 2.8 billion dollars in scholarships a year. [05:40]
- Over a thousand NCAA institutions, about 300 in Division I, 65 in the Power 5 (moderator's figures). [15:21] 351 Division I schools. [15:52]
- At one panelist's former campus, 141 athletes had Pell grants (caption "pill Grant"; the count may be garbled). [16:54]
- Cost of attendance adds 2 to 4,000 beyond the athletic scholarship. [17:56]
- NBA 2005 negotiation set the one-year-after-high-school rule. [22:00]
- Developmental league salary mentioned as "I think 25,000". [25:37]
- 1100 schools play college athletics and 23 turn a profit without subsidy. [31:11]
- 23 coaches paid more than 2.5 million (moderator, "I think it was 23"). [32:11]
- Trust fund of 5,000 dollars per year. [34:46] Caption at [39:56] reads "$55,000", probably garbled.
- Northwestern: 492 athletes, 19 sports (11 female, 8 male); the spending figure "over $800,000" is ambiguous in the captions. [47:40]
- Hypothetical: student body graduation rate of 65 percent used as an example. [56:25]
- NLRB vote described as five votes, possibly three to two. [10:47]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Labor law: employee status under the National Labor Relations Act, then a separate union vote. [10:17]
- Antitrust: the Jenkins case argues scholarship caps restrain trade. [35:48]
- Title IX parity. [33:14]
- Collective bargaining as the route for league age rules. [22:00]
- Federal cost-of-attendance calculation. [18:26]
- Academic Progress Rate (APR) called better than before but a weak standard. [52:50]
- Proposed graduation-rate proportionality: compare athlete rates to the school's own student body. [56:25]

## Limits and open questions

- No data, analytics or models were presented; this is opinion and legal commentary.
- Speakers represent the NCAA, a university, the NBA and a law school; each speaks from an institutional position.
- Outcomes were pending in 2015 (labor board decision, appeal of the antitrust case).
- Captions do not mark speaker changes; some attributions above are by context. Several names, case names ("oanon", "Kesler") and figures are garbled.
- Claim that coaches are the highest paid public employee in 40 of 50 states is garbled ("40 of the highest paid employees and 40 of the 50 states") and unverified. [57:27]
- Predictions at [38:24] to [44:35] are untested.

## Q&A

- Does UAB dropping football signal more schools doing so? Panelists say probably not; it was a unique situation. [46:39]
- Why keep athletic scholarships rather than need-based aid? A panelist says the experience seems similar either way and need-based aid may be discussed. [48:40] [49:12]
- What does reform mean for Olympic sports? Mike says they are on the sidelines now and could be the next phase of legal challenges. [50:15] [50:47]
- How to handle academic standards and the North Carolina lawsuit? Jim says institutions must be accountable; another panelist says one cutoff would hit campuses differently. [51:49] [53:51] [55:24]
- Could graduation targets be proportional to the school's student body rate? Panelists say it has merit. [56:25] [56:55]

type: video-summary

title: "SSAC15: Wearable Technology: Athlete Analytics (Presented by Zebra Technologies)"
event: SSAC15 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Andrew Hawkins (Cleveland Browns), Brian Kopp (Catapult Sports), Kirk Lacob (Golden State Warriors; caption spelling), Eric Petrotinelli (Zebra Technologies; caption spelling), Brian Russell (Zephyr Technologies), Mark McCloskey (moderator, Wired), Amanda Lurie (student host; caption spelling)]
topics: [sports-science, injury-health, american-football, basketball, front-office, decision-making]
confidence: untested
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

A 2015 panel with a Browns receiver, Catapult, the Warriors, Zebra and Zephyr discusses how wearable tracking is used in pro sport. Speakers agree that hardware matters less than turning data into simple, trusted guidance for coaches and athletes. Examples include a hamstring-history player held to a workload ceiling, individualized limits in place of fixed pitch counts, and live substitutions in Australian football. The panel also covers adoption barriers (league equality, device safety, size), contract and labor worries, whether to tell athletes everything, and days lost to injury as the clearest value case. Evidence is anecdotal and several speakers sell the technology.

## Key claims

- Zebra's speaker separates player tracking from consumer wearables, expecting consumer wearables to be dominated by large apparel and tech brands. [04:07]
- Catapult's speaker says the value is in the data and in showing teams value, not in new hardware, and that the US is early in adopting sports science. [04:37] [05:08]
- The Warriors use Catapult, previously used Zephyr, and are trying Zebra with their minor league team. [06:08]
- Hawkins says a teammate with hamstring problems in prior seasons was shut down once his calculated workload reached a set level, and had no hamstring issues that season. [07:10]
- Australian clubs use the devices in games and practice (no pads), and the league uses longitudinal data to find injury-prone situations. [08:13] [08:44]
- Hawkins says the data confirmed that his workload after a coaching change was high, and he was scaled back. [10:47] [11:19]
- Lacob says the front office trusts coaches and trainers to manage players day to day and looks at long-term effects; use is still in its infancy. [11:49] [12:20] [12:50]
- The technology touches the whole organization and coaches must be shown why a change is needed. [13:20]
- Hawkins says a pre-combine analysis found slower 40 times came from coasting through the second step, and sharing video and acceleration data gave a way to fix it, so the technology is not only for restricting athletes. [15:21]
- A simplified load number gives head coaches a shared language, for example asking for a light mechanical day. [16:23]
- Measuring load individually could replace fixed rules like a flat pitch count. [17:23]
- A panelist relays that communication is about 70 percent of the battle and the data about 30. [17:54]
- Data is a tool that often confirms coaches' intuition; the quants-versus-subjective split is a false dichotomy. [18:24] [18:55]
- Zebra's speaker says everything should connect to game day, then to the rest of the week. [20:59]
- Metrics must be explained to fans; physiology is harder to explain than speed and distance. [23:03] [23:33]
- Hawkins expects that after about five years of data the numbers will show decline, and this may affect releases. [25:36]
- Lacob says anything placed on an athlete will be part of labor negotiations, and that data looks backward while management must project. [31:43] [32:13]
- The technology can be delivered live; Australian football makes substitutions from live data, while US college teams view it live without acting on it. [34:16] [34:47] [35:17]
- The NFL plans to have systems in all 31 stadiums the next year, with data kept central for competitive equality, and offensive and defensive coaches differ on who should see it. [37:48] [38:49] [39:49]
- Barriers to adoption include safety of a battery-powered device, and the need for smaller washable units. [40:21] [40:51]
- Hawkins says the hardware is cheap but the service around it costs money; Zephyr's speaker says college engineering students can do analysis as projects. [48:31] [49:01]
- On withholding data, one panelist says athletes do not need to know everything because the data are not always conclusive; others say transparency matters for buy-in, and timing matters. [50:02] [51:32] [52:33]
- Sleep and nutrition are named as the two biggest drivers of performance. [52:33]
- Lacob speculates, and says it is not a fact, that more pick and rolls could relate to knee injuries. [54:34]
- Zebra's system can pass heart-rate data from other vendors' devices over Bluetooth; the panel does not want 18 devices on an athlete. [55:34] [56:04]
- Days lost to injury is a simple metric teams use. [57:35]
- Injury prevention is the clearest way to show dollars of value and reach mass adoption. [1:01:11]

## Numbers and definitions

- Catapult has done this "over eight years". [04:37]
- Hawkins' 16-game season; the capped player had hamstring-derailed seasons for the last three years. [07:10] [07:41]
- Pittsburgh pitchers stop at 120 as an example of a fixed rule; others could go 150 or need to stop at 100. [17:23]
- Communication 70 percent, data 30 percent (relayed remark). [17:54]
- Olympic track: up to three percent speed increase for an 800 meter runner. [44:24]
- Team Oracle catamaran: 72 feet, 40 knots, 30 feet in the air. [44:24]
- A receiver lined up 15 times on the left and three times on the right; every right-side snap was a run. [38:18]
- NFL systems in 31 stadiums next year. [37:48]
- Antonio Bryant story: about 10 million guaranteed, cut within a month or two; panelist says tracking could have saved 8 to 10 million. Hedged ("I think") and unverified. [59:37] [1:00:09]
- Anquan Boldin (caption "bolden") reportedly ran 4.85 (caption "485") at age 21, now 34. Unverified. [28:41]

## Methods and frameworks named

- RFID player tracking and GPS wearables (Zebra, Catapult), remote physiological monitoring (Zephyr).
- Workload thresholds per player; longitudinal data to find injury-prone situations.
- Simplified load or intensity scores for coaches.
- Live dashboards and Australian dynamic substitution.
- Days lost as an outcome metric.
- Data integration over Bluetooth.

## Limits and open questions

- Three of the five panelists work for vendors; claims are commercial and anecdotal. No data, sample sizes or studies were shown.
- The hamstring example is one player; the ACL example [59:07] and Bryant example are single cases.
- Panelists disagree on withholding data: one says some data should not be told, another says if denied he would not wear it. [50:02] [51:02]
- Hawkins says players' feel and data matched, but he did not show a comparison. [10:47]
- Real-time data was not available to North American decision makers at the time. [33:46]
- Auto-captions do not mark speakers; first answers at [03:07] could not be attributed to one panelist. Names garbled in places (Petrotinelli spelled two ways).

## Q&A

- Are these tools affordable for high schools and colleges? Eventually yes; pricing, packaging and service are the barrier. [45:25] [46:27]
- Is there data you would not tell an athlete? Some; timing and transparency matter. [50:02] [52:33]
- How has wearable data helped basketball coaching? Still learning; load capacity and movement types are being studied. [53:34] [54:04]
- Could wearables talk to each other? Yes through integration, but how much is too much. [55:34] [56:04]
- How does injury prevention push the field forward? Days lost and return-from-injury signals. [57:35] [59:07]

## Summary

Two Baylor Applied Performance staff describe how they package GPS, heart-rate and questionnaire data for football coaches. They frame athlete stress with general versus specific adaptation, stacking of risk factors, and use it or lose it. They report that mood, nutrition, soreness, sleep and body weight changed how hard practice felt or how fast athletes ran, separate preparedness (recent exposure) from readiness, use position-specific load metrics, and set weekday loads as a percent of game load. The talk stresses relationships, storytelling and the 22 hours outside practice. Despite the title, it shows little in-game data, no predictive model, and no sample sizes.

## Key claims

- The speakers say their job is to package information so coaches with decades of experience do not need to handle the analytics, and the coaches should trust them to compartmentalize. [02:01] [02:31] [03:01] [07:35]
- Athletes adapt generally to general stress, so high-level athletes need specific stressors. [04:33]
- Injuries come from stacking factors (sleep, nutrition, body weight), not single causes, compared to comorbidity in disease. [05:33] [06:04]
- Qualities fade if not worked: speed needs work every 7 to 10 days and strength about weekly. [06:04]
- They found athletes in a good mood tolerate higher load, and bad mood can make an easy GPS session feel hard. [08:37] [09:07]
- Preparedness should be based on the last three or four weeks of exposure, not on last year's camp. [10:38]
- Readiness covers what the athlete can handle today given recent load; they say a spike is manageable if the athlete is ready. [11:08]
- A wide receiver's speed was half a mile an hour faster at a heavier body weight, which they share with nutrition staff. [11:08]
- Poor daytime nutrition led to soreness, worse sleep and lower body weight the next day, seen over three years. [11:38] [12:08]
- Player load is divided by distance for linemen; high-velocity distance is not used for them; accelerations, decelerations and low-velocity IMA are. [12:38] [13:08] [13:38]
- Left tackles turn outside 70 percent of the time; whether to balance this is debated. [14:10] [14:42]
- Weekly practice load is set as a percent of game load: Tuesday and Wednesday 60 to 70, Thursday 50 to 55. [17:16] [17:48]
- Training is a dose of stress, and both too little and too much fail. [18:20]
- The week is split into the first 48 hours (recovery), the middle 72 (push, and get ahead on schoolwork) and the final 48 (ramp up). [18:52] [19:22]
- They use Catapult and wellness questionnaire data to find habits of the fastest and most powerful athletes, since they have athletes about two hours a day and the other 22 matter. [20:54] [21:24]
- They do not monitor sleep objectively; they use self-report as a way to start conversations. [21:54]
- A well-developed aerobic system helps the body handle load spikes. [23:25]
- Information does not automatically change behavior; stories and relationships do. [23:55] [24:27]
- They look for 1 percent improvements through outside partners. [25:29]
- Takeaways: stress pairing, the psychological side, better storytelling (monster truck and Prius analogy), and a buffer so athletes and the organization never stop. [26:00] [27:32] [28:34]

## Numbers and definitions

- Player load per yard: player load divided by distance. [13:08]
- Speed every 7 to 10 days; strength about once a week. [06:04]
- Example optimal body weight between 198 and 202 (one athlete). [06:04]
- Wide receiver about half a mile an hour faster at 220 pounds or heavier. [11:08]
- Spike tolerance: caption reads "within 25 or 50%" then "spike of 25%"; ambiguous. [11:08]
- Linemen cover about 60 percent of a skill player's distance. [12:38]
- Left tackle turns outside 70 percent. [14:10]
- Saturday game is 100 percent; Tuesday and Wednesday 60 to 70; Thursday 50 to 55. [17:16] [17:48]
- First 48, middle 72, final 48 hours. [18:52] [19:22]
- Athletes seen about two hours a day, 22 hours otherwise. [21:24]
- Fall camp averaged over two to three years as a reference. [09:37]
- Practice rating example: athlete gave 4 and then 2 on 1 to 5 scales against GPS. [08:37] [09:07]

## Methods and frameworks named

- General adaptation and specific adaptation to imposed demands. [04:03]
- Stress pairing (comorbidity). [05:33]
- Use it or lose it. [06:04]
- Catapult GPS (player load, high-velocity distance, IMA, accelerations), heart rate, "a mega wave" (caption spelling, device unclear), wellness questionnaire. [09:07] [21:24]
- Preparedness versus readiness. [10:38] [11:08]
- Weekly load as percent of game load. [17:16]
- Calendar notes covering loading and meals. [16:15]
- Stories and analogies for behavior change. [24:27]

## Limits and open questions

- No numbers, sample sizes, effect sizes or comparison groups; observations are described as seen over three years. [12:08]
- Despite the title, no in-game wearable results or predictive injury model are shown; game load is only the 100 percent reference. [17:16]
- Cannot tell which speaker said what; claims are the Baylor program's own view from 2016.
- Mood and nutrition findings could be correlation with other factors; the speakers describe the mechanisms without testing.
- Spike tolerance claim is garbled in the captions. [11:08]
- Speakers acknowledge two schools of thought on balancing turn direction. [14:42]
- Names of other staff are garbled in captions and are not used here.

## Q&A

No Q&A; the speakers say they are out of time. [29:05]
